profile.name: Duckwalk
profile.tagline: A low-slung rock and roll guitar strut born in blues and medicine shows.
profile.insight: Chuck Berry first used the duckwalk as a child to duck under a table for a ball, and later deployed it on stage to hide wrinkles in his rayon suit.
profile.profile: The duckwalk is a dynamic stage element and physical movement characterized by a low partial squat or a one-legged hop while playing the guitar. Popularized by rock and roll pioneer Chuck Berry in the 1950s, its roots trace back to 1930s blues artists like T-Bone Walker and early 20th-century traveling medicine shows. Beyond its iconic status in rock music, it is also utilized as a physical training and testing exercise by the United States military. Performers execute it by shifting into a profile stance, holding the guitar with the neck forward, and hopping or waddling across the stage.
profile.profile_long:
The duckwalk is a prominent form of stage performance and dance move featuring a low partial squatting position or a one-legged hop routine. According to Levon Helm, traveling medicine shows and music shows such as F. S. Wolcott's Original Rabbit's Foot Minstrels, established in 1911, featured midnight rambles where dancers performed expressive routines that helped inspire rock and roll stage moves. In the 1930s, T-Bone Walker performed dance moves while playing his guitar, helping perpetuate the style.

Ultimately, Chuck Berry made the duckwalk internationally popular and is frequently credited as its inventor. Berry recounted using the movement during his childhood to walk under a table with full-bended knees and a vertical back and head to retrieve a ball. When he performed in New York in 1956, a journalist dubbed it the duck walk, and Berry later noted he used it partly to hide the wrinkles in his rayon suit. He incorporated the move into songs such as 1956's 'rock, rock, rock!' and 1973's 'Sweet Little Rock and Roller'.

Other prominent guitarists adopted and adapted the duckwalk for their live performances. Angus Young of AC/DC incorporated a one-legged hop version into his standard stage show, heavily influenced by Berry. Pete Townshend of The Who, Bo Diddley, Dave Grohl, and Keith Urban also performed variations of the move. In French and Spanish traditions, it is noted as a signature stage move across rock history.

Beyond the concert stage, the duckwalk serves as a physical training exercise designed to strengthen the thighs and ankles while testing balance, flexibility, and agility. It is notably included as one of 25 exercises in the physical test at the United States Military Entrance Processing Command (MEPS). Trainees perform the duckwalk to check for flat feet, pain, and proper ranges of motion, with failure resulting in temporary suspension from the process.

sections.origins_and_history: Tracing back to 1911 traveling medicine shows and F.S. Wolcott's Original Rabbit's Foot Minstrels, the movement was performed by early blues musicians like T-Bone Walker in the 1930s. Chuck Berry popularized it globally during the 1950s rock and roll explosion, using it on stage in New York in 1956. It was subsequently adopted by rock guitarists like Angus Young, Pete Townshend, Bo Diddley, and Dave Grohl.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The movement is executed by assuming a low partial squatting position and walking forwards, or by hopping on one bent leg while extending the other leg forward and swinging the lower leg up and down. Performers sometimes move their heads back and forth like a bird for added emphasis.
sections.music_and_instruments: Performed to rock and roll music. The musician plays the electric guitar with the instrument's neck facing forward and the body resting sideways on the hip in profile.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performed on live concert stages in stage attire such as rayon suits, as well as in military physical testing examination rooms.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Used as a showmanship stunt during rock and roll guitar performances and as a standardized physical fitness and medical screening test for military recruits.

basic_steps: Assume a low partial squatting position
Walk forward maintaining the low stance with back and head vertical
Alternatively, hop on one bent leg
Extend the other leg forward and swing the lower leg in the air

teaching.level_notes: Requires balance, flexibility, and agility; tests range of motion and ankle/thigh strength.
